TOPICS: venture-backed exits, trade sales, IPOs, investment performance, capital efficiency, cross-region comparison, exit multiples, data sources

- More checks to limited partners (LPs) are being written in Europe than ever before (Page 5)

- Data analyzed from 2005 to Q1/2011 for deals over $100M (Page 6)

The chart shows that while supply initially exceeded demand, a significant gap emerged by 2010, with supply falling below demand. Key events are annotated, including an immediate drop in deal flow after the bubble burst, an exit boom starting in 2005, and the market becoming saturated with pre-bubble funds. The main conclusion is that Europe now has the largest inequilibrium of venture capital availability on the planet.

**Text Evidence:**
- "Europe today has the largest inequilibrium of venture Capital availability on the planet"
- "Immediate drop in venture deal flow by 50%"
- "Droves of entrepreneurs run for the woods after bubble burst"
- "Exit boom starting in 2005 started to drive up demand"
- "Market still saturated with pre-bubble VC funds"
- "65 % of all VC funds slide to oblivion"
- "Current supply gap: Major gap in supply of venture capital vs. availability of deals"

**Visual Evidence:**
<chart_summary>Chart 1: Supply-Demand Ratio European Venture Capital - Line graph showing two lines (blue for Supply of Capital, light blue for Demand) from 2000 to 2010. Supply starts at 100 and decreases, while Demand increases, crossing the Supply line around 2008. The area where Supply is below Demand is shaded pink and labeled "Current supply gap." Key points are marked with yellow callouts.</chart_summary>

elements.text: As a result, it is a
buyer's market* in Europe:

"European venture capital is a cottage industry characterised by an insufficient number of private investors (e.g. lack of pension and endowment funds which account for roughly  $65 \%$ of the US VC industry) with the capacity and willingness to invest in venture capital, mainly due to past disappointments and the resulting lack of confidence which still inhibits the European venture industry today."
—Egbert Freiherr von Cramm, Managing Director, Deutsche Bank Private Equity

In the US venture receives substantial funding from university endowments, pension funds and family offices - these three combined are by far the largest contributors and account collectively for more than two third of the US venture capital. In contrast, university endowments within the EU allocate less than  $2\%$  of their assets to private equity as a whole, compared to over  $10\%$  in the US. Also, while there are over 11,000 family offices in the US, there are only 2,500 family offices in the EU.

This page highlights the limitations of the Thomson Venture database for representing the European venture capital industry, emphasizing a very small data set. It states that 21% of funds in the database represent only 15% of the industry, with a significant portion of European funds being inactive or non-reporting. The text explains that unlike in the US, there are no mandatory publication requirements in Europe, leading to underrepresentation of top-performing funds. A 3D bar chart visually compares the number of funds in the database for the US (2,774) and Europe (1,261), illustrating the disparity.

**Text Evidence:**
- The data set in Europe is very small, with 21% of funds in the database representing only 15% of the industry.
- In the US, market publication requirements obligate most GPs to publish financial performance.
- In Europe, 85% of EVCA listed funds have disappeared since the burst of the bubble, and only 10% of the remaining funds are considered active.
- Many top-performing European funds do not publish their financial data in the Thomson Venture database.
- The bulk of European venture fund managers still listed are no longer active, creating a long noncontributing tail.

pages.summary:
This page presents a critical analysis of European venture capital statistics, arguing that published data is misleading due to the lack of reported performance for post-bubble vintages starting in 2004/2005. The main visual element is a 3D bar chart titled "Assembly of NAV, European Venture Funds by Vintage," which illustrates the Net Asset Value (NAV) for funds from different years, distinguishing between realized and unrealized gains. The chart shows a significant drop in realized returns after 2000, with post-bubble vintages (2005-2009) showing 100% NAV but no realized returns yet. The text explains that these newer funds are performing significantly better and are now at an inflection point, as evidenced by recent exits.

**Text Evidence:**
- European Venture statistics are notoriously misleading due to negative bias in official statistics.
- There is almost no reported performance of post-bubble vintages, which started in 2004/2005.
- Post-bubble vintages are significantly better performing and are now at the inflection point.
- The source is Cambridge Associates: Global VC & PE Index and Benchmark Statistics 2009.

**Visual Evidence:**
<figure_summary>Figure: Assembly of NAV, European Venture Funds by Vintage - A 3D stacked bar chart showing the Net Asset Value (NAV) of European venture capital funds by vintage year from 1997 to 2009. The bars are divided into two segments: 'Realized' (blue) and 'Unrealized' (purple). The chart highlights a sharp decline in realized returns after 2000, with post-bubble vintages (2005-2009) showing 100% NAV but no realized returns.</figure_summary>

This page displays two magazine article summaries from The Economist and TIME, both dated in early 2011. The left side features a summary of a February 3, 2011, Economist article titled "Vorsprung durch Exports," which highlights Germany's economic success over the past decade, including its fastest GDP per person growth among G7 nations and a forecast for continued strong performance. The right side presents a summary of a March 7, 2011, TIME article titled "How Germany Became the China of Europe," which attributes Germany's competitiveness to its focus on high-quality specialized products, investment in R&D, and cost-cutting, quoting Stephane Garelli of the IMD.

- The Economist article (Feb. 3, 2011) states that Germany grew at its fastest pace for two decades in 2010.

- The IMF forecasts that Germany will have the fastest growth in GDP per head over the next five years.
- The TIME article (Mar. 7, 2011) quotes Stephane Garelli, director of the world Competitiveness Center at the Swiss business school IMD, saying "Germany is in a very competitive position today, more than ever."
- The TIME article explains that German companies poured money into R&D and cut expenses, churning out specialized products of superior quality.
- The TIME article states that this strategy has kept Germany ahead of emerging economies like China's and helped it benefit from their rapid growth.

The right side presents a summary of a March 7, 2011, TIME article titled "How Germany Became the China of Europe," which attributes Germany's competitiveness to its focus on high-quality specialized products, investment in R&D, and cost-cutting, quoting Stephane Garelli of the IMD.

**Text Evidence:**
- The Economist article (Feb. 3, 2011) states that Germany grew at its fastest pace for two decades in 2010.
- The Economist article notes that over the past decade, Germany had the fastest growth in GDP per person among the G7 club of rich economies.
- The IMF forecasts that Germany will have the fastest growth in GDP per head over the next five years.
- The TIME article (Mar. 7, 2011) quotes Stephane Garelli, director of the world Competitiveness Center at the Swiss business school IMD, saying "Germany is in a very competitive position today, more than ever."
- The TIME article explains that German companies poured money into R&D and cut expenses, churning out specialized products of superior quality.
- The TIME article states that this strategy has kept Germany ahead of emerging economies like China's and helped it benefit from their rapid growth.

This page (Page 39) presents a summary titled "The Sky is the Limit," which highlights key findings about European venture capital. It states that the structure and performance of European VC illustrate the potential of a mature industry, with several European funds achieving top-quartile performance in the post-bubble era. The summary also identifies an imbalance between VC funding supply and investment demand as a driver of competition, and concludes that European VC has emerged with strong fundamentals, benefiting from higher capital efficiency than the US despite operating in an inefficient market.

**Text Evidence:**

- A number of funds based in Europe have achieved US top quartile performance in the post-bubble era.
- The imbalance between VC funding (supply) and investment opportunities (demand) is driving a unparalleled competitive landscape.
- European VC has finally emerged with strong fundamentals within the context of an inefficient market while benefitting from a higher capital efficiency than the US.
